front: Processes vs threads: what is a process, and what does its address space contain?
back:
A process is an instance of an executing program: an application loaded from disk into memory and started, an active entity. Its address space contains:
  • Code
  • Data: the static state available when the process is first initialized
  • Heap: dynamically created state (allocations, intermediate results, data read from files); may have holes the process may not access
  • Stack: dynamically created state that grows and shrinks as functions are called and return (LIFO)

front: Process management: what does the OS store in a process control block (PCB)?
back:
• Process state
  • Process number
  • Program counter
  • CPU registers
  • Memory limits, plus the virtual-to-physical mappings needed for address translation
  • CPU scheduling info (time already run, future time, priority)
  • List of open files
  • And more

front: Processes vs threads: what state is private to each thread, and what is shared?
back: Threads in the same process share the virtual address space: code, data, heap, and files. Each thread has its own program counter, stack pointer and stack, CPU registers, and thread ID.

front: Processes vs threads: contrast memory requirements, communication, and isolation.
back:
• Memory: each process needs its own address space; threads share one, so a multithreaded app needs less memory and is more likely to fit in memory
  • Communication: processes need IPC, which is more costly; threads read/write shared variables
  • Isolation: the OS keeps process address spaces separate; threads share the same mappings, so concurrent access to shared data can cause data races and needs synchronization

front: Context switching: what extra steps make a process context switch more expensive than a thread context switch?
back: Setting up the virtual-to-physical mappings is one of the most time-consuming parts of a process context switch. Threads of the same process use the same mappings, so a thread switch skips that step and is cheaper. A process switch also replaces cached data, so the cache goes from hot to cold (cache access takes a few cycles, memory hundreds); threads share the address space, so another thread's data is often already in the cache.

front: When should you use multiple processes rather than multiple threads?
back:
• Isolation is required: the OS gives each process a separate address space that other processes cannot reach, and data moves only through IPC
  • Fault tolerance matters: one process crashing does not kill the others
  • The application is naturally a set of separate programs, e.g. a web server in one process and a database in another

front: When should you use multiple threads rather than multiple processes?
back:
• Tasks share a lot of state and communicate frequently
  • Low-overhead concurrency is desired
  • Memory footprint is a concern
  • You want to exploit parallelism within a single application

front: Thread creation: what two arguments does the Birrell-model fork take, and where does the new thread start executing?
back: fork(proc, args): proc is the procedure the new thread runs, args are the arguments passed to it (not the UNIX fork). A new thread data structure is created with its program counter pointing to the first instruction of proc. After the fork, both threads can execute concurrently.

front: Thread creation: what does join do?
back: The parent thread blocks until the child finishes. When the child completes, its result is returned to the parent via join, and the child thread's resources are deallocated.

front: Thread creation: in Birrell's paper, what happens to a thread whose procedure returns and that nobody joins?
back: It "quietly evaporates", in effect a detached thread. Birrell notes join is not called very much at SRC, and some thread facilities do not provide it at all.

front: PThreads: give the signatures of pthread_create and pthread_join.
back:
int pthread_create(
    pthread_t *thread,
    const pthread_attr_t *attr,
    void *(*start_routine)(void *),
    void *arg);

int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **status);

front: PThreads: what can pthread_attr_t configure?
back:
• Stack size
  • Scheduling policy
  • Priority
  • System/process scope
  • Inheritance
  • Joinable (vs. detached)
Passing NULL gives the default behavior.

front: PThreads: what is a detached thread and how is one created?
back: A detached thread cannot be joined back into the parent, so the parent can exit early while the child keeps running (Paper, Birrell: an unjoined thread already "quietly evaporates", which behaves like a detached thread. In POSIX, letting other threads outlive main requires pthread_exit(), not detachment). Detach with pthread_detach(thread), or at creation with pthread_attr_setdetachstate(attr, PTHREAD_CREATE_DETACHED) and then pass attr to pthread_create.

front: Thread creation race: why is pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, threadFunc, &i) inside a loop buggy, and how do you fix it?
back: i is shared; by the time the child dereferences the pointer the main thread may have incremented i, so multiple threads can see the same value. Fix: copy i into per-thread private storage (e.g. tNum[i] = i; then pass &tNum[i]).

front: Reader/writer: what do the three values of the resource_counter proxy variable mean?
back:
• 0: resource free; reads and writes allowed
  • > 0: being read; only more reads allowed (count of active readers)
  • -1: being written; no reads or writes allowed

front: Reader/writer: why control a proxy variable with a mutex instead of wrapping the whole read/write in a mutex?
back: Wrapping the entire operation in a mutex would be too restrictive: it would prevent concurrent reads. The resource_counter proxy encodes the resource state, and the mutex protects only the bookkeeping, so multiple readers can proceed at once.

front: Reader/writer: what synchronization constructs does the solution need?
back:
• resource_counter: proxy variable (int)
  • counter_mutex: mutex protecting the proxy
  • read_phase: condition variable signaling reading is allowed
  • write_phase: condition variable signaling writing is allowed

front: Reader/writer: why must the predicate check use while rather than if?
back: Waking from cond_wait is two separate steps: removal from the wait queue, then reacquiring the mutex. Between them another thread can acquire the mutex and change the shared state, so the condition that was true at signal time may be false on wake. The while loop rechecks the predicate after reacquiring the mutex. Using if is a bug.

front: Reader/writer: what is a spurious wake-up (lecture terminology) and how do you reduce them?
back: A thread is woken from a condition variable but cannot make progress, e.g. a writer broadcasts read_phase while still holding the mutex, so the readers are removed from the CV queue only to immediately block on the mutex. They do not hurt correctness (the while loop protects) but waste context switches. Reduce them by calling signal/broadcast after unlocking the mutex when possible.

front: Reader/writer: why broadcast for readers but signal for writers?
back: Multiple readers can proceed concurrently, so broadcast wakes all waiting readers. Only one writer can proceed at a time, so signal wakes a waiting writer. Using broadcast where signal suffices is safe but wasteful; using signal where broadcast is needed is a correctness bug.

front: Reader/writer: lecture framing says the exiting writer wakes both classes. What does Birrell's refined version do?
back: Birrell wakes only one class: broadcast readers if any are waiting, otherwise signal one writer. Waking both is correct but causes spurious wake-ups, since whichever class loses the race for the mutex goes straight back to waiting.

front: Reader/writer: Birrell distinguishes two costs the lectures fold together. What are they?
back:
• Spurious wake-up: waking threads that cannot make useful progress, caused by using Broadcast where Signal would do, or by threads waiting on one condition variable for several reasons
  • Spurious lock conflict: a thread woken inside Wait only to block on the mutex the signaller still holds (the lecture's "spurious wake-up"); avoided by computing doSignal under the lock and signaling after releasing it

front: Threading models: describe one-to-one (1:1), with pros and cons.
back: Each user-level thread has a kernel-level thread associated with it. Pros: the OS sees the user threads and understands that the process is multithreaded and what its threads need; user libraries benefit directly from the kernel's threading support. Cons: expensive, every operation goes to the kernel and pays a system call; limited to the policies and mechanisms the kernel supports; this hurts portability: the application runs only on kernels that provide exactly the support it needs.

front: Threading models: describe many-to-one (M:1), with pros and cons.
back: All user-level threads of a process map onto a single kernel-level thread; a user-level library decides which one runs on it. Pros: portable (everything at user level, not reliant on OS limits and policies); no system calls for thread decisions. Cons: the OS loses insight into application needs (it does not even know the process is multithreaded); if a user thread blocks (e.g. on I/O), the whole process blocks.

front: Threading models: describe many-to-many (M:N), with pros and cons.
back: Some user threads map many-to-one onto a kernel thread while others map one-to-one (unbound vs. bound threads). Pros: best of both worlds; the kernel knows the process is multithreaded, so if one kernel thread blocks it can switch to another and the process proceeds. Cons: requires extra coordination between the user-level and kernel-level thread managers.

front: Solaris threading: what are the three layers, and which is the kernel-visible connecting entity?
back:
• User-level threads (ULTs): managed by the user library, unknown to the kernel
  • Lightweight processes (LWPs): the kernel-visible entity connecting user threads to kernel threads; the "virtual CPUs" the library schedules ULTs onto
  • Kernel-level threads (KLTs): managed by the kernel scheduler

front: Solaris: what is a red zone, per Stein & Shah?
back: An unallocated region of the virtual address space separating thread stacks: the library places an invalid page after each stack it allocates, so a thread that runs off its stack faults and the process is signalled. The error is then associated with the offending thread instead of showing up later when the overwritten thread runs.

front: Solaris: why is KLT data not swappable while LWP data is?
back: KLT data is not swappable because OS services like the scheduler need a thread's information even when the thread is not active. LWP data does not have to be present when the process is not running, so under memory pressure the kernel can swap it out (the stack the KLT points to is also swappable). This supports more threads in a smaller memory footprint.

front: Solaris: does every kernel thread have an LWP?
back: No. Each kernel thread executing on behalf of a user-level thread has an LWP (Paper, Eykholt et al.: system threads and interrupt threads have none).

front: Hard vs. light process state: what is split, and what does the split buy?
back:
• Hard process state: relevant for all user-level threads in the process (e.g. the virtual address mapping)
  • Light process state: relevant only for the subset of user-level threads associated with a particular kernel-level thread (e.g. signals, system call arguments)
When switching between two kernel threads of the same process, the hard state is preserved and only the light state is swapped.

front: Solaris signal handling: why are user-level signal mask changes made the cheap common case?
back: Each ULT has a user-level signal mask and each KLT a kernel-level mask; the library installs itself as the kernel signal handler. Mask changes at the user level happen frequently and are cheap (flip a bit in user space, no system call). The expensive kernel-level correction only runs when a signal actually arrives at a thread that has it masked, which is infrequent. This is optimizing for the common case.

front: Solaris signals: a signal arrives at a running ULT that has it disabled, while another ULT that has it enabled is already running on another KLT. What does the library do?
back: The library's wrapper runs, sees the current ULT cannot handle it, and sends a directed signal to the KLT (LWP) where the enabled ULT is running; the kernel delivers it there and the real handler runs. (If the enabled ULT were only runnable, not running, the library scheduler would swap it in instead.)

front: Solaris signals: what happens when all ULTs have a signal disabled?
back: The library makes a system call to disable the signal in that KLT's mask, then re-sends it to the whole process (Paper, Stein & Shah: to the same LWP if the signal was directed, to the process if undirected). The OS finds another KLT that still has the bit enabled, repeating until every KLT has it disabled. When a ULT later re-enables the signal, another system call re-enables it at the kernel level.

front: Solaris signals (Stein & Shah): how are signal handlers vs. signal masks shared?
back: Only the set of signal handlers is shared by the whole process. Each thread has its own signal mask, and each LWP has its own mask as well.

front: Interrupts as threads: what deadlock problem motivates it?
back: If an interrupt handler runs in the context of the interrupted thread and tries to acquire a mutex that thread already holds, deadlock occurs: the handler cannot proceed until it gets the mutex, and the thread cannot release it until the handler returns.

front: Interrupts as threads: what does the mask-based fix for the handler deadlock do, and what does it cost?
back: Disable the interrupt/signal before acquiring the mutex and re-enable it after releasing, so the handler never runs while the mutex is held; a pending interrupt/signal is handled once re-enabled. Changing the mask costs about 12 instructions per mutex operation. (The simpler fix, keeping handlers free of mutexes, is too restrictive.)

front: Interrupts as threads (SunOS, per the paper): what happens on an interrupt, and what if the handler must block?
back: The kernel does the minimum work to move onto the stack of a preallocated interrupt thread and makes it the current thread; the interrupted thread is pinned until the interrupt thread returns or blocks. Only if the interrupt thread blocks does it save its state and become a full thread. Handling interrupts on the interrupted thread's kernel stack is the traditional UNIX scheme Eykholt et al. replace.

front: Interrupts as threads: give the cost, the saving, and why it is a net gain.
back:
• Cost: ~40 SPARC instructions of overhead per interrupt taken (Lecture framing: the checks and, if necessary, creating a separate thread; Paper, Eykholt et al.: the fixed cost of entering through a preallocated interrupt thread, since no thread is created per interrupt)
  • Saving: ~12 SPARC instructions per mutex enter/exit (no interrupt disable/enable around mutexes)
  • Net: a gain, because mutex operations are far more frequent than interrupts, as long as interrupts don't block too often. A textbook case of optimizing for the common case.

front: Interrupts as threads: which interrupts does SunOS 5.0 not handle as threads?
back: (Paper, Eykholt et al.: interrupts above a tunable "thread level" (normally the maximum priority; lowered, typically to the scheduling clock's interrupt level, only where firmware cannot tolerate the short dispatcher lockout). They are not handled as threads and can synchronize only through spin mutexes and software interrupts.)

front: Adaptive mutexes (Solaris): what is the policy and when does it apply?
back: On a multiprocessor, spin while the recorded owner is running on another CPU (it is likely to release soon); block once the owner is not running. (Lecture framing: information about critical-section length is also used to choose spin or block; Paper, Eykholt et al.: critical-section length is not an input; the adaptive mutex is the default kernel mutex type, MUTEX_DEFAULT, records the owner, and polls whether any CPU's current thread is the owner; on a uniprocessor it always sleeps.)

front: Thread reuse (Stein & Shah): what happens to an exiting detached thread vs. an undetached one?
back: An exiting detached thread goes on death row; the reaper runs when there are idle LWPs or death row is full, and frees the stacks of threads that used library-allocated stacks. The freed stacks are kept for reuse, so the reaping rate affects thread creation speed. An exiting undetached thread goes on a zombie list and is reaped by the thread that calls thr_join() on it.

front: Sizing the LWP pool: what does SIGWAITING do and what is thr_setconcurrency?
back: (Paper, Stein & Shah: the kernel sends SIGWAITING when all LWPs in the process are blocked in indefinite waits; if there are runnable threads, the library creates a new LWP. thr_setconcurrency(n) is a library call (not a system call) that hints the expected concurrency: the library keeps at least n LWPs in its pool (or one per thread if there are fewer than n threads). Growth beyond n comes from SIGWAITING.) (Lecture framing: the application asks for more via a set_concurrency system call, to which the kernel responds by allocating another kernel thread.)

front: Boss/workers: how is the pattern structured and what caps throughput?
back: One boss thread accepts and dispatches work; multiple workers consume tasks from a shared queue and execute each task end-to-end. Throughput is limited by the boss: throughput = 1 / boss_time_per_task.

front: Boss/workers: what are the cons of the pattern?
back:
• Thread pool management overhead
  • Lacks locality: the boss has no insight into what a worker was previously doing, so a worker with a hot cache for a similar task may not get it
Specialized-worker variants add locality and QoS differentiation but make load balancing harder.

front: Pipeline pattern: how is it structured and what caps throughput?
back: The task is divided into stages, each handled by one or more threads; tasks flow through stages sequentially and multiple tasks occupy different stages at once. Throughput is limited by the slowest stage: throughput = 1 / longest_stage_time. Balance it by assigning more threads to the slowest stage.

front: Boss/workers vs pipeline, 11 toy orders (120ms each) on 6 threads: give total time and average per-order time for boss/workers.
back: 6 threads = 1 boss + 5 workers. Waves of 5, 5, 1 finish at 120, 240, 360ms, so total time = 360ms. Average = (5*120 + 5*240 + 1*360) / 11 = 2160 / 11 ~= 196.36ms.

front: Boss/workers vs pipeline, 11 toy orders (120ms each, 6 stages of 20ms): give total time and average per-order time for the pipeline.
back: First order finishes at 120ms; each subsequent order 20ms later. Total time = 120 + 10*20 = 320ms. Order k completes at 120 + (k-1)*20; the sum is 2420, so average = 2420 / 11 = 220.00ms.

front: Boss/workers vs pipeline (11 toy orders): which model wins on which metric?
back: Pipeline has lower total execution time (320 < 360ms). Boss/workers has lower average per-order time (~196 < 220ms). Neither is universally better; it depends on which metric you care about.

front: Pattern formulas: give the throughput and total-time formulas for boss/workers and pipeline.
back:
Boss/workers: throughput = 1 / boss_time_per_task; total time = ceil(num_tasks / num_workers) * time_per_task.
Pipeline: throughput = 1 / longest_stage_time; total time for N orders = time_for_first_order + (N - 1) * longest_stage_time.

front: Flash: compare the four web server architectures (MP, MT, SPED, AMPED) in one line each.
back:
• MP: one process per request; simple, no sync, but large footprint and expensive context switches
  • MT: one thread per request; smaller footprint, cheaper switches, but needs sync and kernel thread support
  • SPED: single-process event-driven; smallest footprint, no switching/sync, but blocks on disk I/O
  • AMPED: event-driven main process plus helper processes for blocking I/O; event-driven efficiency with non-blocking I/O

front: Flash (AMPED): how does the dispatcher decide whether to serve a file locally or hand it to a helper?
back: The dispatcher checks with mincore whether the mapped file's pages are in memory (Lecture framing: the helper reads the file via mmap, then the dispatcher checks mincore; Paper, Pai et al.: the residency check comes first, and a helper is dispatched only if the pages are not resident). If the pages are in memory, a local handler serves it directly with no blocking. If not, the request goes to a helper process via a pipe; the helper does the blocking disk read and notifies the dispatcher (the pipe is a file descriptor, so select/poll picks it up). The main loop never blocks on disk I/O.

front: Flash: what does the helper actually send back, and why not the file data?
back: (Paper, Pai et al.: both the main process and the helper mmap the file. The helper touches every page to bring it into memory, then notifies the main process via IPC that the file can be sent without blocking. It never sends file data; the main process sends from its own mapping.)

front: Flash: why are helpers separate processes rather than kernel threads?
back: Back then the kernel was not multithreaded, so the helpers had to be processes (AMPED; the multithreaded equivalent is AMTED). Helpers fake asynchronous I/O instead of relying on native support, which helps portability. Only one helper is needed per concurrent blocking I/O operation, not per request, keeping the footprint below MP/MT.

front: Flash: name the three application-level caches.
back:
• Cached files (data caching)
  • Pathname-to-file lookups (computation caching)
  • Response headers (file-dependent; valid as long as the file has not changed)

front: Flash: what is the byte position alignment optimization?
back: (Lecture framing: an optimization for the network hardware, alignment for DMA and DMA with scatter-gather; Paper, Pai et al.: when writev() sends a response header followed by file data, the OS copies the regions into a contiguous kernel buffer, and a header whose length is not a multiple of the word size misaligns every later copy. Flash pads response headers to multiples of 32 bytes, targeting systems with 32-byte cache lines.)

front: Flash experiments: how were Flash-SPED, Flash-MT, and Flash-MP built, and why that way?
back: Every implementation except Apache included the optimizations Flash introduced, over otherwise identical code. The comparison is therefore really between the models (MP, MT, SPED) and AMPED, not implementation quality. (Paper, Pai et al.: Flash-MT used 64 threads, each handling a whole request.)

front: Flash experiments: name the main workloads used.
back:
• Synthetic (best case): all requests for the same file, varying size, so it is always cached; the generator also allows worst-case and "what if" analysis
  • Owlnet trace: student web sites; small, typically fits in memory
  • CS trace: Rice CS department server; large, does not fit in memory (disk-bound)
Real traces give a realistic access distribution that can be replayed to reproduce the experiment.

front: Flash best-case (synthetic, cached) result: who wins and why does architecture barely matter?
back: All implementations show similar curves: bandwidth rises sharply with file size, then plateaus. SPED is best; Flash is similar but pays its per-request mincore memory check, which buys nothing here. MT/MP are lower (Lecture framing: synchronization and context switching; Paper, Pai et al.: only extra kernel overhead, such as context switching, since MP needs no synchronization). Apache is lowest (no optimizations).

front: Flash best-case: what is the Zeus anomaly?
back: Zeus drops in performance after around 125 KB, from a misalignment in some of its DMA operations (Lecture framing: the dip as read off the Solaris graph the lecture shows; Paper, Pai et al.: the paper discusses a Zeus anomaly only on FreeBSD, for files between 10 and 100 KB, and attributes it to the writev byte alignment problem that Flash avoids by padding headers).

front: Flash Owlnet trace (small, mostly cached): who wins and why does Flash edge SPED?
back: Flash slightly outperforms SPED. SPED blocks when a file isn't cached (no helpers, no async I/O); Flash's helpers handle the occasional disk I/O without stalling the main loop. Both beat MT/MP; Apache remains lowest.

front: Flash CS trace (large, disk-bound): who wins and why?
back: Flash wins: its footprint is smaller than MP's or MT's, so more memory is available for caching files and headers, fewer requests need blocking I/O, and its single address space needs no explicit synchronization. SPED drops below MP and MT because it blocks on disk reads. MT beats MP because it has a smaller footprint (more memory available to cache files) and is able to synchronize more quickly/cheaply (Paper, Pai et al.: MP needs no user-level synchronization between requests, so synchronization is an MT-only cost; MP still performs well on this disk-intensive trace).

front: Flash optimizations experiment: what were the four configurations, and what did it show?
back: Flash with no optimizations; caching only pathname lookups; pathname lookups plus files via mmap; all optimizations (adds cached headers). Connection rate decreases with file size, but rises with each optimization; fully optimized Flash is highest at every file size. Apache, the one implementation without them, performed worst in both trace experiments.

front: Flash: what is the consistent theme across the workloads?
back: When data is cached, SPED smokes AMPED Flash (Lecture framing: Flash's memory check is unnecessary; Paper, Pai et al.: SPED only slightly outperforms), and both beat MT/MP, which pay synchronization and context switching. When the workload is disk-bound, Flash beats SPED (which blocks on I/O) and MT/MP, because its smaller memory footprint leaves more memory for caching and it needs less context switching.

front: What are the three key roles of an operating system?
back:
1. Hide hardware complexity via abstractions (file, process)
  2. Manage underlying hardware resources (allocate memory, schedule the CPU, control access of applications to the various devices in the system); roles 1 and 2 summarize as abstract and arbitrate
  3. Provide isolation and protection so no application interferes with another

front: OS concepts: distinguish abstraction, mechanism, and policy with an example.
back:
• Abstraction: a simplified representation of a resource (process, thread, file, socket, memory page)
  • Mechanism: an operation on an abstraction (create and schedule for processes and threads; open, write, allocate for files, sockets, pages)
  • Policy: a rule for how mechanisms are used to manage the hardware (LRU page replacement, the maximum number of sockets a process may have)
Example: a mechanism that tracks how memory has been accessed (frequency or last-access time) supports LRU, LFU, or random replacement as policies.

front: What does separation of mechanism and policy mean?
back: How you enforce a policy should not be coupled to the policy itself. Incorporate flexible mechanisms that can support a number of policies, e.g. a memory management mechanism that generalizes to LRU, LFU and random. In different settings, different policies make more sense.

front: What does "optimize for the common case" mean and why is it valuable?
back: Understand the context the OS will run in: where it will be used and on what machine (CPUs, memory, devices); what the user will execute; and what the workload requires and how it actually behaves. Knowing the common case, which can change between contexts, lets the OS pick the right policy, which relies on general mechanisms.

front: Optimize for the common case: how do the SunOS interrupt-as-threads numbers illustrate it?
back: Interrupts as threads add ~40 SPARC instructions per interrupt (paid infrequently; Lecture framing: the checks and, if necessary, creating a separate thread; Paper, Eykholt et al.: the overhead of taking an interrupt on a preallocated interrupt thread) but save ~12 instructions per mutex enter/exit (collected on every lock/unlock). Because mutex operations vastly outnumber interrupts, the net instruction count drops, as long as interrupts don't block too often.

front: What happens during a user-kernel mode crossing?
back:
1. The hardware supports the transition, e.g. a trap when an application in unprivileged mode tries to perform an instruction, or a memory access, for which it doesn't have permission, or a system call; the CPU privilege bit is set for kernel mode
  2. The execution context changes from the user process to that of the kernel, arguments are passed, and control jumps to a location in kernel memory
  3. The return does it in reverse, ending at the exact user instruction where the call was made
Cost: the transition takes 50 to 100ns on a 2GHz Linux box, and the OS's content displaces the application's in the cache (cache access a few cycles vs. hundreds of cycles for memory).

front: How are user and kernel mode distinguished, and what happens if user mode tries a privileged operation?
back: They are distinguished in hardware by a CPU bit. In kernel mode the bit is set, allowing any instruction to manipulate hardware directly. In user mode the bit is not set, and attempts at privileged operations are forbidden, triggering a trap.

front: What are the reasons a user-kernel mode crossing happens?
back:
• System calls: the application requests an OS service or privileged access (open, send, malloc)
  • Traps: the hardware traps a privileged instruction or illegal execution in user mode and transfers control to the OS
  • Interrupts: external devices (I/O devices, timers, other CPUs) notify the CPU and need kernel-level handling
In the other direction, the OS sends signals to notify the application.

front: What is a kernel trap and why does it happen?
back: When a privileged instruction is encountered during non-privileged (user mode) execution, or when an application in unprivileged mode tries to perform an instruction, or a memory access, for which it doesn't have permission, the application is trapped: its execution is interrupted and the hardware transfers control to the OS at a specific location. The OS then checks what caused the trap.

front: What are the steps during a kernel trap?
back:
1. A user process attempts a privileged instruction in user mode (privilege bit not set)
  2. The hardware interrupts the application's execution
  3. The hardware transfers control to the OS at a specific location (kernel mode)
  4. The OS checks what caused the trap
  5. The OS decides, per its policies, whether to grant the access or terminate the process

front: What is a system call?
back: An operation in the interface the OS exposes so an application can get privileged access to hardware resources, or have the OS perform a service on its behalf. Examples: open (file), send (socket), malloc (memory; strictly a C library function that uses the brk/mmap system calls). All OS services are made available through system calls.

front: What are the steps during a system call?
back:
1. The application writes the arguments and saves relevant data at a well-defined location (arguments passed directly or by address)
  2. It makes the call using a specific system call number
  3. The execution context changes from user to kernel mode and control jumps to the kernel code for that call; the kernel uses the number to know how many arguments to expect and where to find them
  4. The kernel performs the operation, e.g. accessing the hardware
  5. Control and any results return to the process, back in user mode, ending back at the exact instruction in the user process where the call was made from
In synchronous mode the process waits until the call completes.

front: OS designs: contrast monolithic, modular, and microkernel on structure and performance.
back:
• Monolithic: everything included: abstractions and all services packaged at the same time; compile-time optimizations (inlining); but too much state and code, hard to maintain, debug and upgrade, and large memory requirements (which can impact performance)
  • Modular: basic services plus dynamically installed modules behind a defined interface; easier to maintain and upgrade, smaller footprint, fewer resources; the indirection can reduce some optimization opportunities (typically not a significant performance impact)
  • Microkernel: only an address space and a thread in the kernel, everything else at user level; small size and verifiability, but bad portability and expensive frequent user/kernel crossings via IPC

front: OS designs: what are the pros and cons of a microkernel?
back: Pros: size (lower overheads, better performance); verifiability (valuable where correct behavior is critical, like some embedded devices or certain control systems). Cons: bad portability (often customized to the underlying hardware); harder to find common OS components due to specialized use case, leading to software complexity; expensive frequent user/kernel crossings, because file systems and drivers run at user level and communicate with the kernel via IPC.

front: Process vs thread: what defines a process, and what do threads share?
back: A process is defined by its virtual address mapping (code, data, heap) and its execution context (registers, stack, PC); each has its own address space and PCB. Threads live within a process, sharing its address mapping (code, data, heap, files) but each has its own execution context and thread control block.

front: Context switch: what makes a process switch expensive, split into direct and indirect cost?
back: Direct cost: CPU cycles to load and store PCBs to and from memory. Indirect cost: the cache goes from hot to cold, so the incoming process's data is not cached and accesses go to memory (hundreds of cycles vs. a few for cache). A thread switch keeps the same virtual-to-physical mappings, skipping one of the most time-consuming parts, and keeps the cache warmer.

front: Process lifecycle: name the five states.
back:
1. New: being created; admission control, PCB allocated/initialized
  2. Ready: ready to execute, not currently executing
  3. Running: scheduled and executing on the CPU
  4. Waiting: waiting on an I/O operation or an event
  5. Terminated: exited, with or without error

front: Process lifecycle: list the state transitions.
back:
• New -> Ready: PCB created/initialized
  • Ready -> Running: scheduler dispatches onto the CPU
  • Running -> Ready: preempted by the scheduler
  • Running -> Waiting: initiates I/O or waits on an event
  • Waiting -> Ready: I/O completes or the event occurs
  • Running -> Terminated: process exits

front: Thread lifecycle: for what reasons does a thread wait?
back:
• Waiting to be scheduled on the CPU (ready queue)
  • Waiting to acquire a synchronization construct (blocked on a mutex)
  • Waiting for a condition to become true or a signal (on a condition variable wait queue)

front: Thread lifecycle: what is a zombie thread and who cleans it up?
back: A thread that has exited but whose data structures have not yet been freed. Exiting threads go on death row, and a special reaper thread periodically frees them (Lecture framing: a structure requested before reaping can be reused; Paper, Stein & Shah: the reaper frees detached threads on death row; undetached threads go on a zombie list and are reaped by the thread that calls thr_join()).

front: List the steps for a process to transition from waiting (blocked) to running.
back:
1. Process sits on an I/O/event queue in the kernel
  2. The I/O completes or event occurs; the device/event notifies the kernel
  3. Kernel moves it from the I/O queue to the ready queue (now ready)
  4. The scheduler selects it from the ready queue
  5. The currently running process is preempted; its PCB saved to memory
  6. The OS dispatches the waiting process: loads its PCB into registers
  7. The process is now running on the CPU

front: IPC: how much is the OS involved in message-based vs shared-memory IPC?
back: Message-based: the OS is involved in every send/recv (system calls). Shared-memory: the OS is involved only during setup (mapping shared physical pages into both address spaces); after that it is out of the way.

front: IPC: give the pros and cons of message-based IPC.
back: Pros: the OS manages the channel and provides the same APIs (system calls) to both sides for send/recv, so neither process implements the protocol itself. Cons: overhead; every piece of information is copied from the sender's address space into kernel memory, then into the receiver's address space.

front: IPC: give the pros and cons of shared-memory IPC.
back: Pros: after setup the OS is out of the fast path, so individual reads and writes incur no OS overhead. Cons: mapping memory between two address spaces is expensive, so it wins only if the setup cost is amortized across enough messages (for a few exchanges, message passing can be better); the APIs message passing provides have to be reimplemented, and without a well-defined API the code tends to be more error-prone.

front: Multithreading benefits: list the main ones.
back:
• Parallelization across multiple CPUs
  • Concurrency / hiding I/O latency: switch to another thread while one blocks
  • Specialization and hot caches
  • Lower memory footprint than multiprocess
  • Cheaper communication (shared variables vs IPC)
  • Cheaper context switching than processes

front: Multithreading: when does adding threads become pure overhead?
back:
• When all threads are CPU-bound and there are already as many threads as CPUs: extra threads only compete for CPU time and add context-switching overhead
  • When the work is not parallelizable (serial dependency chains)
  • When synchronization overhead dominates (too much contention on shared locks)
Switching threads hides idle time only if t_idle > 2 * t_ctx_switch.

front: Multithreading: when is it useful to add more threads for I/O-bound work?
back: When threads perform many I/O operations, idle time can be hidden by switching to another thread, so long as t_idle > 2 * t_ctx_switch. (Also useful when you have fewer threads than CPU cores.)

front: Multithreading: what are the sources of overhead?
back:
• Thread creation/destruction (allocating structures, stack space)
  • Context switching (still consumes CPU cycles)
  • Synchronization (primitives cost cycles and memory; contention serializes execution)
  • Memory (each thread needs a stack and control block)

front: Boss/workers: contrast the two dispatch mechanisms.
back:
• Direct signaling: the boss tracks idle workers and sends work to a free one. No sync among workers, but the boss does more work per task, lowering throughput.
  • Shared queue: the boss enqueues; idle workers pull. The boss does less per task, but synchronization is needed on the queue. More common.

front: Boss/workers: how can you improve throughput or response time?
back:
1. Increase the number of workers (use a pre-allocated, dynamically sized thread pool)
  2. Decrease the boss's work per task (shared queue rather than direct signaling)
  3. Use specialized workers to exploit locality and improve per-task time

front: Boss/workers: what are the limiting factors on performance?
back:
• The boss: throughput is limited by the boss's time per task (1 / t_boss), and a full queue increases it
  • Synchronization on the shared queue: the boss producing and the workers contending for the front
  • Thread pool management overhead
  • Lack of locality: the boss does not know what each worker did last

front: Pipeline: how can you improve throughput, and what limits performance?
back: Improve by giving the slowest stage more threads (e.g. three times the threads for a stage that takes three times as long), sizing stages with a thread pool, and passing work through shared buffers, which absorb small imbalances between stages. Limits: throughput is set by the weakest (longest) stage; the pipeline is hard to keep balanced over time (input rate changes, a stage's resources run out); and synchronization points at multiple stages add overhead.

front: What is a mutex (minimum contents and behavior)?
back: A mutual exclusion lock ensuring only one thread at a time accesses a critical section. It has at minimum a lock status, an owner, and a list of blocked threads. When a thread locks it, it has exclusive access; others blocking on the same mutex wait until the owner releases it.

front: What is a condition variable and how does it relate to a mutex?
back: A condition variable is used with a mutex to control execution on arbitrary conditions beyond locked/unlocked. A thread can wait (atomically releasing the mutex and sleeping); another can signal (Lecture framing: wake one waiting thread; Paper, Birrell: at least one, possibly more) or broadcast (wake all). A woken thread automatically reacquires the mutex before returning from wait.

front: Reader/writer with writer priority: what extra state and checks are added?
back: Add int waiting_writers = 0;. A reader waits while resource_counter == -1 || waiting_writers > 0. A writer increments waiting_writers on entry, waits while resource_counter != 0, then decrements it. In the writer's exit, signal write_phase first, then broadcast read_phase.

front: Reader/writer: why is the default solution already reader-priority?
back: A new reader only blocks when a writer is currently active (resource_counter == -1), not when a writer is merely waiting. So readers proceed as long as no writer holds the resource.

front: Can you always avoid spurious wake-ups? Give the lecture answer and Birrell's refinement.
back: Lecture: No. If the decision to signal depends on shared state, that state must be read under the mutex, so the signal or broadcast must also happen inside it. (Paper, Birrell: only the test of shared state needs the mutex; compute it into a local (e.g. doSignal = (i == 0)) inside the lock and signal after unlocking.)

front: What is the most ideal way to prevent the T1/T2 deadlock, and why does it work?
back: Maintain a lock order: all threads acquire mutexes in the same order (e.g. A before B). To lock B a thread must already hold A, so the other thread cannot hold A, has not reached its first lock, and cannot hold B: no cycle in the wait graph is possible. Foolproof, but hard to enforce across a large code base.

front: Deadlocks: besides lock ordering, what strategies exist?
back:
• Get all locks up front and release them at the end, or use one mega-lock (limits parallelism)
  • Prevention: check each acquire for deadlock and delay it or restructure the code (expensive)
  • Detection and recovery: find cycles in the wait graph and roll back (expensive, sometimes impossible)
  • Ostrich algorithm: do nothing; if it deadlocks, reboot

front: Kernel vs user threads: how does the Linux 1:1 (NPTL) model handle scheduling, synchronization, and signaling?
back:
• Model: NPTL is 1:1, one kernel task per user-level thread
  • Scheduling: the kernel sees every user thread and schedules it directly
  • Synchronization: the kernel sees whether each thread is blocked on synchronization; going through the kernel costs a user/kernel crossing, which is affordable because kernel trapping is now much cheaper
  • Signaling: the kernel sees each thread's signal mask and delivers signals directly to the right task, so no user-level mask juggling between ULTs and KLTs is needed

front: Kernel vs user threads: in the Solaris M:N model, what are the two levels of scheduling?
back: The user-level library schedules unbound ULTs onto LWPs (Paper, Stein & Shah: from its pool, by priority, process scope); the kernel scheduler schedules the kernel threads onto the CPUs (Paper, Stein & Shah: system scope). (Paper, Stein & Shah: the library grows the pool via SIGWAITING and the thr_setconcurrency hint.)

front: Why are the Solaris concurrency/signaling/LWP mechanisms not needed in Linux NPTL?
back:
Linux NPTL is 1:1: every user thread has its own kernel task, which the kernel sees. Solaris's LWP layer, its concurrency mechanisms (Paper, Stein & Shah: thr_setconcurrency and SIGWAITING), and user-level signal mask routing existed to keep the number of kernel threads small. That is no longer needed because
  • kernel trapping is much cheaper, so user/kernel crossings are affordable
  • modern platforms have more memory
  • the kernel sees every user thread

front: What is an interrupt vs a signal (source, dependency, timing)?
back: An interrupt is generated externally by components other than the CPU (I/O devices, timers, other CPUs), appears asynchronously, and depends on the hardware platform. A signal is triggered by the CPU and software, can be synchronous (SIGSEGV, SIGFPE) or asynchronous (SIGKILL, SIGALARM), and depends on the operating system.

front: How does the OS know what to execute on an interrupt?
back: The device sends an interrupt signal (or MSI message) to the CPU, identified by its number. The CPU looks the number up in the system-wide interrupt handler table maintained by the OS and sets the program counter to the corresponding handler. Interrupt handling is per-CPU, with per-CPU masks.

front: Can each process configure its own signal handler? Can each thread?
back: Each process can: the OS keeps a per-process mapping from signal number to handler, and the process installs handlers via signal()/sigaction() (some signals cannot be caught). Each thread cannot: the set of handlers is shared by the whole process. Each thread can set its own signal mask (Paper, Stein & Shah: all threads share one vector of handlers; only masks are per-thread).

front: Solaris threads: which thread handles an incoming signal, and what if every thread masks it?
back: The kernel delivers it to a KLT whose mask has it enabled. The library wrapper passes it to the current ULT if its mask allows it; otherwise it swaps in a runnable ULT that has it enabled, or sends a directed signal to the KLT running one. If every ULT masks it, the library disables the kernel masks one by one via system calls and re-issues the signal until all are disabled; it stays pending until a ULT re-enables it.

front: What is the problem if an interrupt or signal handler needs to lock a mutex?
back: The handler runs in the interrupted thread's context on its stack. If that thread already holds the mutex and the handler tries to lock the same mutex, deadlock occurs: the handler can't acquire it (the thread holds it) and the thread can't release it (it is suspended while the handler runs on its stack).

front: SunOS interrupts-as-threads: how is the cost of dynamic thread creation avoided?
back: The kernel pre-creates and pre-initializes thread structures for the interrupt routines it supports, pointing them at the handler and allocating their data upfront. (Paper, Eykholt et al.: on an interrupt it does the minimum work to move onto the preallocated thread's stack; converting it into a full thread happens only if the handler blocks on lock contention.)

front: Why did the SunOS paper reject the explicit top/bottom (two-level) handler split?
back: The bounded first-level handler that wakes a second-level thread would require restructuring device drivers and would always cost a full context switch. The SunOS approach instead pays the thread cost only under contention: no handler code runs on the interrupted thread's stack, the whole handler runs in the interrupt thread, and that thread is promoted to a full thread only if it blocks.

front: Stein & Shah: what is the signal-mask workaround for a handler needing a mutex?
back: Disable (mask) the signal before acquiring the mutex and re-enable it after releasing, so the handler never runs while the mutex is held; a signal arriving in between stays pending and is handled once re-enabled. In the lightweight threads library a ULT changes its mask at user level with no system call; the kernel mask is corrected only when a signal actually arrives.

front: Flash MP vs MT: contrast memory footprint, caching, and isolation.
back: MP: simple (spawn the same process several times), but a higher memory footprint, costly shared state through IPC, and difficulty having several processes listen on one port. MT: shared address space and state, lighter memory requirements, and no system calls for threads to coordinate; but it needs explicit application-level synchronization. Caching: MP's larger footprint leaves less memory for caching files; MT's smaller footprint leaves more. Isolation: MP processes have separate address spaces, so one failing does not affect the others; MT threads share one, so one thread crashing can bring down the whole process.

front: Flash MP vs MT: what kernel support and context-switch differences matter?
back: MT depends on OS-level support for threads (less of an issue now than in the past); MP needs none. MT gets a cheap user-level context switch within the shared address space; MP pays the high cost of a process context switch.

front: Flash MP vs MT on the disk-bound CS trace: what did the experiments show?
back: (Lecture framing: MT does better than MP because its smaller footprint leaves more memory for caching files, reducing disk reads, and because it synchronizes more cheaply; Paper, Pai et al.: MP processes need no user-level synchronization between requests, so synchronization is an MT-only cost, and MP still performs well on this disk-intensive trace.) Flash performs best.

front: Flash AMPED: how does it handle a file-cache miss, and what does the helper return?
back: A single-threaded event dispatcher detects events (via select/poll); handlers run to completion. Flash checks with mincore whether the mmaped file pages are in memory. On a miss it hands the request to a helper process via a pipe (Paper, Pai et al.: the helper touches the pages to bring them into memory and returns only a completion notification (not the data)).

front: Flash: list the benefits of the AMPED event-based model over MT and MP.
back:
• Single address space and single flow of control: lower overheads
  • Smaller memory footprint (one helper per concurrent blocking I/O operation, not an entity per request)
  • More memory left for caching
  • No context switching overhead
  • No synchronization
  • Simpler programming (no reasoning about shared access)
  • Fakes asynchronous I/O with helpers, so it is portable

front: Flash: what are the limitations of the AMPED event-based model?
back:
• Works well for server-type applications, but is not necessarily applicable to arbitrary applications
  • Event routing on multi-CPU systems adds complexity (events must be steered to the right CPU)
  • Asynchronous I/O is not available everywhere, so helpers are needed to avoid blocking the whole process
  • Jumping among handlers hurts locality and pollutes the cache (far less than a context switch)
  • The mincore memory check is unnecessary work when everything is cached

front: Flash: would you convert AMPED to AMTED, and how would it compare?
back: Yes: replace helper processes with helper threads (AMTED, the multithreaded equivalent), now that kernels are multithreaded. Helpers would share the address space, giving a lighter footprint and cheaper context switches than processes. (Paper, Pai et al.: the gain is limited because there is only one helper per concurrent blocking I/O operation and it returns only a notification.) Caveat: shared state between helpers and the dispatcher needs synchronization.

front: Flash experiment 1 (synthetic best case): what question did it answer and how was it structured?
back: Question: what does performance look like when every request is a cache hit? Setup: all requests ask for the same file, varied in size from 0 to 200 KB, so it is always cached after the first access. Varying file size varies work per request; the single file guarantees hits, isolating server overhead from disk I/O. Takeaway: when cached, model differences are small, but event-driven models have a slight edge.

front: Flash experiment 2 vs 3 (Owlnet vs CS trace): what distinct questions did each answer?
back: Owlnet: how do servers perform on a realistic small workload that mostly fits in memory? (Flash and SPED lead; Flash edges SPED on the occasional disk access.) CS trace: how do they perform on a realistic large workload that does not fit in memory? (SPED collapses; Flash wins via its small footprint and helpers.)

front: Class project: as you add threads for a trace of many requests for a single file, what happens?
back: Once read, the file stays cached, so every request is served from memory. Adding threads first increases throughput sharply (more concurrency, no disk bottleneck), then plateaus at a high value as the CPU becomes the bottleneck or context-switching overhead offsets the gains.

front: Class project: as you add threads for random requests across a huge pool of large files, what happens?
back: The working set far exceeds memory, so the server is disk-bound from the start. Adding threads gives modest improvement by hiding disk latency, then plateaus quickly once the disk is saturated at a much lower throughput. Beyond that, extra threads add switching overhead, contention, and consume memory that could cache files, possibly decreasing throughput slightly.

text: In the Birrell/PThreads model, a thread is created with a {{c1::fork}} call taking a procedure and its arguments, and a parent waits for a child with {{c2::join}}, which returns the child's result.
extra: (Paper, Birrell: if a thread's procedure returns and nobody joins it, it quietly evaporates.)

text: The reader/writer solution uses a proxy variable where {{c1::0}} means free, a positive value means readers are active, and {{c2::-1}} means a writer is active.
The first two OS roles, hiding hardware complexity and managing hardware resources, are summarized as {{c1::abstract}} and {{c2::arbitrate}}.
extra: The third role is providing isolation and protection.

text: Pipeline throughput is 1 / {{c1::longest_stage_time}}, while boss/workers throughput is 1 / {{c2::boss_time_per_task}}.
